contributions.headingText: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC) is an invasive carcinoma composed of mixed mucinous, intermediate (transitional), and squamoid neoplastic cells arranged in solid and cystic patterns.
2C60 & XH1J36 Carcinoma of breast, specialized type & Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
MEC can affect any breast quadrant; when arising in the retroareolar region, it can cause nipple discharge {28043647}.
Breast MEC usually arises in adult women ranging in age from 29 to 80 years {22135628}. One case has been described as a secondary tumour in a patient treated for lymphoma.
MEC is quite frequent in the salivary glands, but it rarely affects the breast, with < 40 cases reported to date {22135628}.
MEC can present as a solid nodule or a cystic lesion. The reported size ranges from 0.6 to 11 cm {22135628}.

Similarly to its salivary gland counterpart, breast MEC can show a wide range of histological features, spanning from low-grade to high-grade lesions {22135628; 14634807; 28043647}. Grading can be performed by applying the salivary gland or the breast grading systems, with similar results {14634807}. Low-grade MEC more frequently shows a cystic component. Cystic spaces are lined by mucous cells intermingled with eosinophilic cells. Solid areas show neoplastic cell nests with a peripheral layer of basaloid cells gradually merging in groups of epidermoid cells and mucous cells. High-grade MECs are more frequently solid, and they show the same cell composition as their low-grade counterparts. In high-grade MEC, cytological atypia is present, mitotic figures are numerous, and necrosis can be present. Intermediate-grade breast MEC has been occasionally reported {14634807}. An intraductal component can be present {14634807; 24166608}. True keratinization with squamous pearl formation is not a feature of MEC of either low or high grade.

Immunohistochemistry is helpful in identifying the different cell types. Specifically, high-molecular-weight cytokeratins (e.g. CK14) and p63 stain basaloid and epidermoid cells, whereas low-molecular-weight cytokeratins (e.g. CK7) stain the mucous cells {14634807; 2480681; 24166608}. This gives rise to a peculiar zoning pattern of positivity similar to that observed in MEC of the salivary glands {14634807; 12021929}. Breast MECs retain the GATA3 and mammaglobin positivity observed in other breast tumours {30380176}.

The cytological features have rarely been reported, but they seem to be similar to those observed in the corresponding salivary gland lesions; FNA specimens can show cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm intermixed with mucinous and basaloid cells. In addition, mucous material can be present in the background. Diagnosis can be difficult when salivary gland–like tumours are not considered {16930336}.

Almost all reported breast MECs have been included among the triple-negative breast carcinomas, lacking ER and PR expression and ERBB2 (HER2) amplification. Recently ER, PR, and AR positivity was described in a subpopulation of the neoplastic cells {29390541; 30380176} of low- and intermediate-grade breast MEC. Few data have been reported on the molecular features of breast MEC. The t(11;19)(q21;p13) translocation, resulting in fusion of CRTC1 (MECT1) and MAML2 and considered typical of low-grade salivary gland MEC {27068311; 27340278}, has been investigated in two cases of breast MEC, which harboured partial deletion of 11q21 (MAML2) {19200580} and CRTC1-MAML2 fusion, respectively {30380176}.
Essential: presence of basaloid, epidermoid, and mucous cells; absence of true keratinization.
MEC is staged according to the criteria adopted for other types of breast carcinomas.

Grading is the most important histopathological prognostic factor for breast MEC. Grading can be performed using the criteria usually applied to breast cancer, as well as those for MEC of the salivary glands {14634807; 22135628; 30380176}; both grading systems are based on architecture, cellular atypia, and mitotic count. Similar to its salivary gland counterpart [[El-Naggar AK, Chan JKC, Grandis JR, et al., editors. WHO classification of head and neck tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2017. (WHO classification of tumours series, 4th ed.; vol. 9). http://publications.iarc.fr/548.]], high-grade MEC of the breast shows solid architecture, nuclear anaplasia, and a high mitotic count, often associated with necrosis and lymphovascular infiltration {22135628}.

According to a recent review of the literature {22135628} based on 26 cases with follow-up information, none of the low- or intermediate-grade MECs led to the patient’s death. Only one case among the low-grade MECs recurred as high-grade disease, but the patient was alive and well 156 months later {12440816}. One recent case of low-grade MEC was reported to show metastatic deposits in 3 of 18 axillary nodes, but the patient was alive and well 156 months after surgery {29390541}. In contrast, all high-grade MECs showing axillary and/or distant metastases lead to the patient’s death {22135628}.
